description:
AniNow is an agri-innovation team exploring how NASA data, AI, software, and geospatial tools can address challenges in agriculture, climate resilience, and food security. We aim to turn complex Earth observation data into practical, user-friendly solutions. We are composed of members with skills in GIS, remote sensing, data science, AI/ML, web development, UI/UX, agriculture, and environmental science.

Our team is based in Laguna, with graduates from UPLB and De La Salle University.
summary: AniNow Klima helps Filipino farmers decide what to plant after harvest. A farmer picks the field's location, the crop grown now (rice, any of 28 other crops, or fallow), the harvest and next planting dates, drainage and water source. The model replays 44 past seasons (1981–2024) of daily NASA POWER weather for that place and checks each of 29 crops against published FAO limits for temperature, water, soil pH and soil texture, using a measured soil sample for the site or the farmer's own soil test, and the FAO-56 crop water method. A season's score is its weakest condition. The tool reports how many past seasons each crop would have had what it needs, how much extra water it would have required, and why. In our test case, a rice field harvested in November, a suitable crop exists at 17 of 22 Philippine sites; the best alternative needs a median 573 mm less irrigation than a second rice crop; and where the soil rules everything out, the tool says "no suitable recommendation" instead of guessing. The model has no fitted parameters, every threshold is traced to a source, and its statistical weaknesses are published alongside its results.
details:
Dashboard:

AniNow Klima — Your next planting

What it does.

The farmer gives the field's location, the crop grown now, the harvest and next planting dates, whether water stays on the field, and whether there is irrigation. Location is one of 22 sites, each with its own weather record and tested soil sample; a farmer's own soil test can replace the sample. The current crop can be any of the 29 crops, or fallow. For each of 29 crops the tool returns whether it fits the window, in how many past seasons its requirements were met, how much water it was short of, which condition limits it, and when to plant.

How it works.

S = min(temperature, water, soil pH, soil texture)

W = min(1, rain / ETc)

ETc = sum over the cycle of Kc(day) x ETo(day)

ETo = 0.0023 (Tmean + 17.8) sqrt(Tmax - Tmin) Ra

Crops that cannot fit the window or the field's drainage are excluded before scoring. A season with S ≥ 0.6 is a good year. Nothing is trained or fitted.

The condition scores use the four crop limits published in FAO EcoCrop; crop water need (ET_c) and reference evapotranspiration (ET₀, the Hargreaves–Samani equation) follow FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 (Allen et al., 1998); taking the weakest score is Liebig’s law of the minimum, as used in FAO land evaluation; the 95% interval is Wilson’s (1927); and the water ratio W and the 0.6 pass mark are our own choices.

Results.

Test case: rice as the current crop, harvest 15 November, next planting 31 May, rainfed.

Planting date

Second rice crop: 964 mm short. Mungbean: 44 mm short.

22 sites

A crop is suitable at 17 sites; none at 5.

Water saved

Median 573 mm (5,725 m³/ha) less than rice, at all 22 sites.

Limits and Descriptive Analytics

No harvest record exists for these fields, so no accuracy figure is reported.

Benefits and intended impact. Advice specific to one field, soil and window; each result names its limiting condition and source; "not rated" and "no suitable recommendation" are valid answers. The aim is a second income from idle land with less irrigation risk.

Tools. Python standard library (model, statistics, local form) · matplotlib, NumPy, pandas, Jupyter (figures) · FastAPI on Render (API) · web front end on Vercel.

Creativity and factors considered. The tool replays history instead of forecasting, so a farmer hears "22 of the last 41 seasons". We considered window fit, drainage, missing satellite data (never read as zero), shared weather grid cells, and which constants are our own.
